title: How Much Should You Save for an Emergency Fund in Nepal?
metaDescription: Calculate how much you need in an emergency fund in Nepal. Recommended 3 to 6-month buffer guidelines, ideal bank accounts, and liquidity rules.
h1: How Much Should You Save for an Emergency Fund?
directAnswer: In Nepal, an emergency fund should equal 3 to 6 months of mandatory living expenses for salaried employees with stable jobs, or 6 to 9 months for business owners, freelancers, and commission-earners. This money must be parked in liquid, insured Class A commercial bank savings accounts or flexi-fixed deposits, completely isolated from stock investments or real estate.
author: Lalitpur Advisory Research Desk

sections.h2: Sizing Your Emergency Buffer Based on Income Stability
sections.contentHtml:
An emergency fund is insurance, not an investment. Its sole objective is protecting your family from unexpected shocks: medical emergencies, sudden vehicle repairs, or temporary job transitions.

Employment ProfileRecommended Fund SizeSample Household (NPR 60k/mo expenses)
Dual-Income Salaried Household3 Months Essential Living ExpensesNPR 180,000
Single-Income Salaried Household6 Months Essential Living ExpensesNPR 360,000
Entrepreneurs & Freelancers6 to 9 Months Essential ExpensesNPR 360,000 - NPR 540,000

sections.h2: Where Should You Keep Emergency Savings in Nepal?
sections.contentHtml:
Never invest your emergency fund in NEPSE equities, mutual funds, or illiquid land. Instead, hold it across:

  • Tier 1 (Instant Liquidity): 1 month of expenses in a Class A commercial bank savings account with debit card and mobile banking enabled.
  • Tier 2 (High-Yield Safety): 2-5 months in auto-sweep recurring fixed deposits or easily breakable term accounts insured up to NPR 500,000 under the Deposit and Credit Guarantee Fund (DCGF).

Ready to structure your household reserves? Review our structured personal savings roadmap.

faqs.question: Are bank deposits in Nepal safe for emergency funds?
faqs.answer: Yes. Deposits in licensed commercial banks (Class A) are regulated by Nepal Rastra Bank, and individual deposits up to NPR 500,000 are guaranteed under the Deposit and Credit Guarantee Fund (DCGF).
